To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the median metallicities of G- and K-type dwarfs in the solar neighborhood differ by 0.2-0.3 dex; and (2) the median metallicites of G- and of K-type stars having the same median velocity dispersion about the Galactic center also differ by 0 2-0. 3 dex.

(1) the stellar metallicity distribution functions of long-lived G and K main-sequence stars in the Milky Way are different, and that (2) the metallicity distributions are different even when the stars are selected to have the same median rotational velocities.

(i) the median metallicity, [Fe/H], of G-type dwarves is systematically higher than that of K-dwarfs having the same velocity dispersion, (ii) the metallicity distribution function of G- and K-dwarfs are different, and (iii) the difference in the median metallicity between G- and K-type dwarfs decreases as the velocity dispersion increases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the evolution of the Milky-Way's stellar halo, and the formation of its metal-rich and metal-poor components, as revealed by the kinematics and metallicities of its main-sequence stars.
the question of whether the metallicity of main-sequence stars is conserved over long timescales, as is generally assumed.
understanding how stars form and evolve in the context of their galactic environments, by analyzing the chemo-dynamic properties of nearby metal-pool halo stars on the main-sequence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stellar metal abundances, [X/H], are not conserved over time and are not the same for stars of different spectral types.

metal-poor main sequence stars of different effective temperatures (or spectral types) have different chemo-dynamicals, and that the difference is not due to observational selection effects, or to differences in their ages, but to the fact that the metal-poor G-type dwarfs have been accreting metals onto their surfaces from the interstellar medium, while the K-type dwarfs have not.
there is evidence for the accretion of metals onto the surfaces of main-sequence stars, and that the rate of accretion depends on stellar mass and metallicity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the stellar metal abundance ratios, [X/Fe], are not conserved over time, but rather, they are subject to time-dependent accretion and/or diffusion processes that depend on stellar mass, effective temperature, and possibly on the elemental abundance ratio, X. We
the metallicity distributions for main-sequence G- and K-type stars in the Milky Way halo/thick disk are not identical, as is usually assumed in analyses of chemo-dynamically tagged stars.

the metallicity distribution of long-lived, metal-poor stars is not a one-dimensional function of [Fe/H], but instead is a multi-dimensional function of [X/H] that depends on the stellar effective temperature.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stellar metallicities of metal-poor stars on the main-sequence are not conserved, and the metallicity-kinematics correlations for long-lived stars of different masses are not the same.
the chemo-dynamics of long-lived stars may be more complex than previously thought.

, for the first time, we are able to detect a systematic difference between the chemo-dynamic distribution function of metal-poor G- and K-type main-sequence stars, which implies that their metallicities are not strictly conserved over time, and that they are subject to metal accretion.
